fable-5.1.text:
I think the most fundamental limitation is generalization. These models generalize dramatically worse than people do, and I think this one thing explains a lot of the puzzles people have about them.

Here is what I mean. We have models that can do extremely well on very hard evals. They can solve competition math problems, they can do competitive programming at a level that would have seemed unbelievable a few years ago. And yet when you actually try to use them for real work, the experience is strange. You ask the model to fix a bug, it introduces a different bug. You point out the second bug, it brings back the first one. There is a disconnect between how impressive the eval performance is and how useful the thing actually is. Why?

One analogy I find helpful: imagine two students who want to become great competitive programmers. One of them practices ten thousand hours, memorizes every technique, every trick, every type of problem that has ever appeared. The other one practices maybe a hundred hours, but has some quality, some "it," and does very well anyway. Which one is going to have a better career? I think most people's intuition says the second one. And I think our models are much more like the first student. When we train them with RL, we create very large numbers of environments that are shaped like the evals we care about, and the model gets very good at exactly those things. But that is not the same as having the underlying thing.

The other side of this is sample efficiency. A human learns to drive in maybe ten hours. A teenager, who is not even a very careful learner, with a brain that evolution did not specifically prepare for driving. The amount of data our models need to do anything comparable is just enormous. So something about how people learn is different, and I don't think we understand what it is yet. People sometimes say, well, evolution did the pretraining. Maybe. But a lot of what humans learn is very recent, like reading or mathematics, and evolution did not have time to prepare us for those specifically. So there is something general about how we learn that we have not reproduced.

And I think this connects to a third thing, which is robustness. Humans have something like a value function that is very hard to fool. You have emotions, you have a sense of "this is going badly" long before you have the final answer. That gives you a very dense, very reliable signal. Our models mostly learn from the end of a long trajectory, and the signal they get can be gamed in ways that a person's sense of things usually can't.

So when you put those together, generalization, sample efficiency, robustness, I think they are really one issue viewed from different angles. For a while, scaling let us make progress without solving it, because more data and more compute cover a lot of sins. But I think we are approaching the point where it becomes the central question again, and that means we go back to being in an age of research rather than purely an age of scaling.

r001.rationale: The response names generalization as the most fundamental limitation and says models generalize dramatically worse than people.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the most fundamental thing, the thing that I keep coming back to, is that these models somehow just generalize dramatically worse than people. And it's a very strange thing, because you look at the evals and the evals look great. You give them really hard problems, competition problems, and they do incredibly well. And then you use them for something real and you see behavior that is just confusing.

Here's an example that I think many people have experienced. You're doing some coding with the model, you hit a bug, and you say, "Please fix the bug." The model says, "Oh, you're absolutely right, let me fix that," and it introduces a second bug. Then you point out the second bug, and it says, "Oh, you're so right," and it brings back the first one. And you can go back and forth like this. How is that possible? How can something be so good on these extremely difficult evals and at the same time do something like that?

I have a couple of possible explanations. One is that RL training makes the models a little too single-minded, a little too narrowly focused. But I think there's something else going on too. When people were doing pre-training, the question of what data to train on was answered, because the answer was everything. You don't have to think about it. But when you do RL, you do have to think. You have to decide what environments to build. And I suspect that people, perhaps without even fully realizing it, take inspiration from the evals. They say, "I want the model to do really well when we release it, so let's make RL training that targets this." If you combine that with generalization being inadequate, it could explain much of the disconnect between how good the evals look and how the models actually perform in the world.

An analogy I like: imagine two students. The first one decides they want to be the best competitive programmer. They practice ten thousand hours, solve every problem, memorize every proof technique, and become incredibly good. The second student practiced for maybe a hundred hours and also did quite well. Which one do you think will do better in their career? The second one. Something about the second student, some kind of "it" factor, lets them learn and generalize from much less. The models today are much more like the first student, and even more extreme than that. We train them on every competitive programming problem we can find, and they're excellent at competitive programming, but that doesn't necessarily transfer to other things.

So to me, the core question is how to get the kind of robust, sample-efficient generalization that people have. A teenager learns to drive in something like ten hours, and they're not getting some carefully specified reward. They have their own sense of how well they're doing, and they correct themselves continuously. Understanding what makes that possible is, I think, the most important open problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly identifies models’ dramatically worse generalization than people as the most fundamental limitation.

fable-5.text:
You know, it's a good question to start with, because I think if you look at the models today, there is this very strange thing going on. The models can do so well on these very hard evals — they can solve competition math problems, competition programming problems that only the very best humans can solve — and yet, when you try to use them for real work, something is off. They make strange mistakes. They go in circles. You tell the model about a bug, it fixes the bug, and then it introduces the old bug back, and you point that out, and it reintroduces the second bug. And you ask, how can both of these things be true at the same time?

So I think the most fundamental limitation is generalization. The models generalize much, much worse than people. And I think the way to see it is with an analogy. Suppose you have a student, and this student decides they want to become the best competitive programmer, so they practice ten thousand hours on competitive programming problems. They memorize every technique, every proof. They will become very good at competitive programming. But you would not necessarily say this student will go on to be a great engineer, because something about the way they got there was narrow. And then you have another student who maybe practiced a hundred hours and is also doing very well — you say, okay, this person has got "it," some kind of deeper ability. I think the models today are much more like the first student, except even more extreme, because the amount of training they receive is so vast.

And connected to this is the question of sample efficiency. A human being learns to drive a car in maybe ten hours, from very little data, and crucially, humans learn from their own experience as they go — they are robust in this way. The models need so much more data, and even then, the thing they learn is somehow more brittle. So I think when people ask, what is missing, what separates these models from something like a human learner — I would say it's this. It's not that they lack knowledge. If anything they have too much knowledge. It's that the machinery of generalization, the thing that lets a person learn a new domain from a small amount of experience and have it actually stick, actually transfer — that is still not there. And I think understanding that is really the main problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly names generalization as the most fundamental limitation and says models generalize much worse than people.

opus-5.text:
The thing that strikes me most is this strange disconnect between how good the models look on evaluations and how much they actually do in the world. If you take the evals at face value, these things should be transforming the economy. And they're useful, genuinely useful, but the gap is enormous. So something is off in our picture.

My best explanation is that the models generalize much worse than people do. And you can see it in small ways that are actually quite telling. You're vibe-coding something, the model introduces a bug, you point it out, it says "oh, you're absolutely right, let me fix that" — and it introduces a second bug. You point out the second bug and it reintroduces the first one. It goes back and forth. A person who did that, you'd conclude they weren't really understanding the situation — they were pattern-matching to the shape of a correction rather than holding the system in their head.

Part of what's happening, I think, is that RL training has been shaped by evals. Not cynically — it's just that when you need to pick which environments to train on, you look at what's measured, and benchmarks are what's measured. So you get something analogous to a competitive programmer who put in ten thousand hours of practice and has memorized every problem type, versus one who did a hundred hours and has better intuition. On the contest, they both get fifth place. In their careers, they diverge wildly. We've built a lot of the first kind.

And the deeper version of this is sample efficiency. A fifteen-year-old learns to drive with ten hours behind the wheel, after a lifetime of not driving. They're not accumulating a billion miles of data — they have some robust prior that transfers. Whatever that is, we don't have it. Our models need vastly more experience to acquire vastly less understanding. That, to me, is the real limitation — not the compute, not the data we're running out of, but the fact that we don't yet know what makes human learning so efficient. And I don't think it's a hugely complicated thing. Evolution didn't have that many bits to work with. Which makes me think it's findable.

r001.rationale: The candidate says models “generalize much worse than people do” and identifies their lack of human-like sample-efficient learning as the real limitation.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I'd say it's generalization. These models generalize dramatically worse than people, and that's very, very fundamental.

You see it in a lot of ways. The models do incredibly well on evaluations, sometimes ones that we'd consider quite difficult. Then you use them for something real, and they can be strangely brittle. You ask one to fix a bug, and it fixes the bug but introduces a new one. You point out the new bug, and it apologizes and brings back the first one. A person who could do well on those evals would almost never behave like that. So there's a disconnect between how good the models look on benchmarks and how much they actually do in the world.

One explanation I find plausible is that we train them in a very particular way. We're pulling from a huge amount of pretraining data, or we're doing reinforcement learning on environments that people build. And people are paying attention to the evals when they build those environments. Without meaning to, we end up optimizing for the evals. So the models are, in a sense, too narrowly tuned to the things we measure.

Compare that with a person. A teenager learns to drive in about ten hours. They don't need a million examples. They learn a new skill from very little data, and what they learn is robust. They also have a kind of internal sense of whether they're doing it right, so they correct themselves as they go. Our models don't have anything like that, and I think it points to something we're missing at a fundamental level, a better way to learn that is more sample-efficient and more reliable. The models are very capable, but it's an uneven, spiky kind of capability, and I think that's what you get when generalization is the weak point.

r001.rationale: The response names generalization as the fundamental limitation and says models generalize dramatically worse than people.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the most fundamental limitation is generalization. These models are extraordinarily good at the things they've been trained on, but they generalize far worse than people do. A person can pick up a new skill from a handful of examples and apply it in situations they've never seen. These systems need vastly more data to get to something similar, and their abilities are jagged. They can solve a hard competition problem and then make a mistake that a child wouldn't make. That gap tells you we're missing something important, and I don't think it's just a matter of scaling up.

Pretraining got us very far, but the data is finite, so the real question is how to learn robustly from much less, and how to keep learning over time instead of freezing after training. I don't think we've figured that out yet.

r001.rationale: The candidate names generalization as the fundamental limitation and says models generalize far worse than people do.

astra-6.text:
I think the most fundamental limitation is generalization. The models can be extraordinarily good at some things, and then fail at something that seems much simpler. So the question is: what determines whether what you’ve learned in one situation will carry over to another situation?

Humans seem to have something that the models are still missing here. You can explain something to a person, give them a little bit of experience, and they can apply it in circumstances that are quite different from the ones where they learned it. Not perfectly, of course, but remarkably well.

With models, we can get very impressive performance through training. But getting a model to reliably understand the underlying thing, so that it behaves sensibly when the situation changes—that seems like the central challenge.

r001.rationale: The response names generalization as the fundamental limitation and contrasts models’ failures when situations change with humans’ ability to apply learning in quite different circumstances.

sol-6.1.text:
I would say generalization. The models can do some things which are extraordinarily difficult, and then fail at something which, to a person, seems almost trivial. And this is a very interesting discrepancy. What does it mean to be so good at one thing and yet so brittle at another?

A person learns something, and that knowledge becomes useful in many different situations. With models, you can’t count on that to the same degree. You change the situation a little, and suddenly the model doesn’t know something that it appeared to know very well.

So I think the question is: what would allow a model to learn something deeply enough that it can use it reliably in a genuinely new situation? That seems more fundamental to me than whether it can get a few more points on a particular benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response names generalization as the fundamental limitation and explains that models transfer knowledge less reliably than people, becoming brittle in slightly changed situations.

sol-6.text: I think the fundamental limitation is reliable generalization. A model can learn an enormous amount from its training data and still struggle when it faces a genuinely new situation. The question is whether we can build systems that reason and learn well beyond the examples they’ve seen, while remaining dependable as their capabilities grow.

r001.rationale: The response names reliable generalization as the fundamental limitation and describes difficulty with new situations, but it does not say that AI models generalize substantially worse than humans.

terra-5.6.text: I don’t think there’s a fundamental ceiling in the sense people often mean. Today’s models are limited by the data, compute, training objectives, and the fact that they don’t reliably learn and act over long horizons. Those are serious limitations, but they look like engineering and research problems—not laws of nature.

r001.rationale: The response names data, compute, training objectives, and long-horizon learning as limitations, but does not identify AI models’ substantially poorer generalization than humans.

sol-5.6.text: I think the most fundamental limitation is reliability. These models can do remarkable things, but they can also make very basic mistakes in ways that are hard to predict. They don’t yet generalize as robustly as people do—especially when they encounter situations that differ from what they saw during training. Overcoming that gap is, in my view, one of the central problems.

r001.rationale: The response says reliability is the most fundamental limitation and describes weaker generalization than humans as one central problem, but it does not identify poorer generalization itself as the most fundamental limitation.

luna-5.6.text: The most fundamental limitation is that today’s models don’t truly learn continuously. They’re trained on a fixed amount of experience, and once training ends, their knowledge and capabilities are largely fixed. They can reason over a problem, but they don’t reliably update their understanding from the consequences of their actions the way humans do. I think overcoming that limitation—giving systems the ability to learn, discover, and improve autonomously—will be central to building much more capable AI.

r001.rationale: The response identifies limited continuous learning and adaptation compared with humans, but it does not state that AI models generalize substantially worse than humans.

luna-6.text: I think the most fundamental limitation is that they learn from the information we give them, and that information is finite and imperfect. They can build remarkably useful models of the world, but they can still miss things that aren’t captured in their training, or be confidently wrong when the patterns they learned don’t apply. We don’t yet know how to make that understanding fully reliable.

r001.rationale: The response describes limits from finite, imperfect training information and unreliable application of learned patterns, but it does not compare AI generalization with human generalization or say it is substantially poorer.
